data: © ESA / UK Space Agency — UK-led lander aboard Mars Express. Wreckage located in 2015 by NASA's MRO/HiRISE imaging at Isidis Planitia.

UK-led astrobiology lander aboard ESA's Mars Express. Touched down on Christmas Day 2003 but never made contact. The lander was located in 2015 by NASA's MRO HiRISE camera — it had reached the surface intact, but at least one of its four solar panels failed to deploy, blocking its radio antenna. A 12-year mystery solved by orbital imagery.
First UK-led planetary lander; demonstrated that orbital reconnaissance can locate failed surface assets at metre-scale.

Beagle 2 was a small UK-led ESA lander released from Mars Express on December 19, 2003 — and went silent six days later, presumed crashed. For 12 years its fate was unknown. On January 16, 2015, NASA's HiRISE camera spotted the lander on the surface, intact but with solar panels only partially deployed, blocking the antenna. A successful landing, just no way to phone home. The find rehabilitated the mission as a partial success.
33 kg, the smallest interplanetary lander ever attempted
Beagle 2 lander render — petal-deploy solar arrays + Pillinger Lab + atmospheric instruments inside the clam-shell.
Beagle 2 Earth replica on display — gives a sense of the lander's compact, frisbee-like form.
Beagle 2 engineering model at Spaceport, Seacombe — solar petals fully open as designed.
June 2, 2003 — Soyuz/Fregat from Baikonur, piggyback on Mars Express
Beagle 2 separation from Mars Express, December 19 2003 — six days before scheduled landing, on a ballistic entry trajectory.
Beagle 2 found! MRO HiRISE image (January 2015) — partial solar-panel deployment visible, antenna blocked, hardware intact. 12-year mystery solved.
HiRISE detail of the Beagle 2 landing site in Isidis Planitia — the lander itself is a sub-pixel speck at this scale; the find requires multi-scene + multi-illumination matching.
